artists/hans-richter.title: Hans Richter
artists/hans-richter.content:
Hans Richter
German painter and filmmaker, active in the Dada groups in Zurich, Berlin and New York. His book Dada: Art and Anti-Art is used in this wiki as background only, and his claims are attributed to him. Source note: richter-dada-art-and-anti-art.
Film

ghosts-before-breakfast (1928): his film with music by several composers. The film is linked, not embedded, until its licence is checked.

Points from the book

Richter describes the Zurich years from the inside. The early pages of the book (pp. 11–20) cover this. Treat his account as one participant’s view.
His account of Duchamp contrasts with Cravan’s. Artist note: Marcel Duchamp.

Lens notes

Artist: a painter who moved into film, so his work gives the medium lens a clear case.
Medium: painting and film. Use the film note to compare how the two forms handle chance and movement.

To check

 Dates (1888–1976) against a biography.
 Any claim about the film’s aims is Richter’s own statement. Check it against a second source before presenting it as fact.

artworks/anemic-cinema.title: Anémic Cinéma
artworks/anemic-cinema.content:
Anémic Cinéma
A short black-and-white, silent film made by Marcel Duchamp in 1926. The Museum of Modern Art’s record describes it as six minutes long, originally shot on 35mm and later transferred to video.
Watch

Your browser cannot play this video. Download the file.

Rights. This is the Wikimedia Commons file “Anemic Cinema.webm” (uploaded 2022). Commons marks it as public domain in the United States, because it was published before 1 January 1929. The Commons page credits the copy to a restoration by Aeon Video on YouTube. Whether the film is out of copyright in Australia has not been confirmed. The restoration may carry its own rights. Check both before the wiki is used in Canvas.
Records. Museum of Modern Art, New York. MoMA’s own transfer is not used here. MoMA’s rights page says its video cannot be licensed by MoMA.
Lens notes

Medium: a silent film with no story that students can follow. The question for students is what a film can do without narrative or sound. Discuss this as a question, not as a settled reading.
Artist: Duchamp’s practice moved between painting, objects and film. Related method: ready-made, which also asks what the artist’s choice does.
Historical: made in Paris in 1926, about ten years after Dada began in Zurich.

To check

 The Commons video plays in the wiki and in Canvas. (Not loaded from the build sandbox. Test on the live site.)
 Australian copyright status of the original film, and of the restoration.
 Who worked on the film with Duchamp. The MoMA record names Duchamp as creator only. Check a catalogue before naming collaborators.

artworks/ghosts-before-breakfast.title: Ghosts Before Breakfast
artworks/ghosts-before-breakfast.content:
Ghosts Before Breakfast
Hans Richter’s film, released on 14 July 1928 according to Wikipedia. Its credits include Darius Milhaud and Paul Hindemith, who wrote music for it. The title in German is Vormittagsspuk.
Watch (linked, not embedded yet)
The full film is on the Internet Archive: Vormittagsspuk (Ghosts Before Breakfast), 1928. Wikipedia links to this item.
It is not embedded yet, because the item page could not be checked from the build sandbox. Before adding an embed, check the item’s licence and that the copy is complete. Then add the embed using the item’s identifier.
Rights
Films made in 1928 are very likely out of copyright in Australia. Restorations, and new music added later, can carry their own rights. Check the Internet Archive item’s licence statement, not only the film’s date.
Lens notes

Medium: a film built on ordinary objects that behave oddly. Related work: anemic-cinema, made two years earlier in Paris. Watch the film itself before teaching this point.
Artist: Richter’s work across painting and film. Artist note: hans-richter.
Historical: made in 1928, after the Dada groups in Zurich, Berlin and Paris had largely broken up. Students can decide, using the sources, whether it continues Dada or is a separate project.

To check

 Release date against a film catalogue. Wikipedia gives 14 July 1928.
 Licence on the Internet Archive item, then add the embed.
 Credits, against a catalogue entry.

index.title: Dada and Surrealism: a test wiki
index.content:
Dada: a test wiki
This is a working test of the wiki model. Four lenses shape how the material can be filtered:

Historical: the period and political conditions behind the work
Social: audiences, institutions, reception and everyday life
Artist: the people, their practice and their networks
Medium: the form the work takes

Use the explore page to filter the notes by lens and medium, or follow links from any note.
Some notes include film, sound or images. Each one states its rights on the page. Where a note only links out, it says so and does not embed the item.
Richter’s account is used as background throughout. Where a note relies on it, the note says so.

methods/ready-made.title: Ready-made
methods/ready-made.content:
Ready-made
An ordinary manufactured object, chosen by an artist, given a short sentence or title, and presented as art. The choice is the act. Marcel Duchamp’s ready-mades are the reference case.
Duchamp’s account
Richter quotes Duchamp’s own statement (p. 89). Duchamp says the choice was based on “visual indifference” rather than on aesthetic pleasure. The short inscribed sentence was meant to move the viewer’s mind “towards other regions, more verbal” instead of describing the object.
Duchamp’s examples include a bicycle wheel fixed to a kitchen stool, a bottle-rack, a urinal (later submitted as Fountain), and a snow shovel inscribed “in advance of the broken arm” (New York, 1915).
Richter’s reading
Richter argues that looking at an object made it art, and that Duchamp’s method was more systematic than the use of found objects by Arp, Schwitters and Janco. He reads the urinal as saying “art is a trick”. This is Richter’s interpretation, and other historians read the ready-made differently.
Lens notes

Artist: the method is tied to Duchamp’s practice and choices.
Medium: the ready-made moves the question from making to choosing, which matters for any medium.

To check

 Dates of each ready-made, against a museum or catalogue record.
 Fountain (1917): the original is lost, and the status of replicas needs a museum record. [Verify.]
 Any image of a ready-made needs its own source note. Mark it “unverified” until the rights are checked.

places/291-new-york.title: 291 (gallery and journal, New York)
places/291-new-york.content:
291 (gallery and journal, New York)
The gallery at 291 Fifth Avenue, run by the photographer Alfred Stieglitz. It showed photography and modern painting together. The journal Camera Work was renamed 291 in 1915.
Points from Richter

Richter describes a “personal union” between artistic photography and modern painting at the gallery. He says it prepared the public for modern art.
The 1913 Armory Show brought European modern art to New York. Richter gives a visitor figure of over 100,000. [Verify against a museum or archive source.]
Francis Picabia’s 1913 satire on abstract art and his “Aesthetic Comment” in the Armory Show catalogue put him near the centre of the group.
From 1915, 291 published Picabia’s attacks on art. Richter says Stieglitz followed the anti-art current, but “the central ideas of Dada lay beyond his sphere of interest”.

Lens notes

Social: who came to the gallery, who was published, and how the public reacted to the Armory Show.
Historical: New York on the eve of the First World War.
Medium: photography as a modern art form, shown alongside painting.

To check

 Gallery dates and address.
 The Armory Show visitor figure.
 Picabia’s 1913 and 1915 publications, against a primary source or catalogue.

sources/dickerman-dada-seminars.title: The Dada Seminars (Dickerman, ed., 2005)
sources/dickerman-dada-seminars.content:
The Dada Seminars (2005)
Edited by Leah Dickerman with Matthew S. Witkovsky. Published by the National Gallery of Art, Washington, as CASVA Seminar Papers 1. The preface is by Elizabeth Cropper and the introduction by Dickerman. Each chapter is by a different scholar, and the chapters are short essays on specific works and moments.
Chapter cited in this wiki

T.J. Demos, “Zurich Dada: The Aesthetics of Exile” (from p. 7). Cited in the note on karawane.

Use in this wiki

Role: a recent scholarly source. Use it for arguments and for short quotations with a page reference. Its essays are one scholar’s reading each, not a general account of Dada.
Rights: in copyright. Quote short phrases only, with a page reference. Do not reproduce the figures on the public site. Link to the institutions named in the captions instead.
Figures: the captions name the Getty Research Institute and the New York Public Library as holders. Check each record before linking.

sources/richter-dada-art-and-anti-art.title: Dada: Art and Anti-Art (Hans Richter)
sources/richter-dada-art-and-anti-art.content:
Dada: Art and Anti-Art (Hans Richter)
Hans Richter (1888–1976) was a painter and filmmaker who took part in Zurich, New York and Berlin Dada. The English edition was translated by David Britt and published by Thames & Hudson.
Use in this wiki

Role: a primary account from inside the group. Richter has a stake in how the story is told, so his claims are attributed to him, and dates and attributions are checked against other sources.
Original: Dada: Kunst und Antikunst, Cologne: DuMont Schauberg, 1964. [Verify the title and publisher against a library record.]
Edition: Thames & Hudson, London. Copyright page: ”© 1964 DuMont Schauberg, Cologne; this edition © 1965 and 1997 Thames & Hudson Ltd, London”. ISBN 0-500-20039-4.
Rights: in copyright. Quotations are kept short and no illustrations are reproduced. [Copyright term to be verified with the library.]
Language: the text contains dated and racialised language and generalising claims. These are not quoted here.

texts/karawane.title: Karawane
texts/karawane.content:
Karawane
A sound poem by Hugo Ball, performed at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916. It is made of invented syllables rather than dictionary words. Ball called this kind of work Verse ohne Worte, verse without words. T.J. Demos quotes this phrase in the Dickerman catalogue essay.
Listen (linked, not embedded)
These recordings are on the PennSound page for Dada sound recordings, which lists them. The page gives no rights statement for the recordings, so they are linked only.

Jerome Rothenberg, with Jean-Charles François and Bertram Turetzky, “Karawane” (about 1985).
Christian Bök, “Karawane” (2009, Getty Research Institute event).

PennSound: Dada sound recordings
Before embedding any of these, check the rights with PennSound and the performer.
Lens notes

Medium: the poem works through sound alone. Each performance changes with the voice, the pacing and the audience. Demos argues that this is a way of giving up the shared meaning of language. This is his argument, not a general claim.
Historical: written in Zurich during the First World War. Demos argues that the sound poems carry the damage of the war, and that Ball’s exile from Germany shaped the poem. Treat this as one reading among several.

To check

 Date of the poem and its first performance, against a catalogue or the Ball diary.
 Rights for each recording before any embed.
 A short, cited quotation is enough for the text. Do not reproduce the whole poem from a secondary source.
